text: In AI safety, what does "alignment" mean?
options: Steering a system toward a person's intended goals
Making a model's outputs line up in a fixed column
Ensuring two models trained on the same data agree
Converting research results into engineering requirements
answer: Steering a system toward a person's intended goals
explanation: An aligned system advances what you actually intended, and a misaligned one pursues something else while looking like it is cooperating. The hard part is that intentions are not formally specified anywhere, so the entire practical problem is the gap between the goal you can write down and the goal the system infers.

text: Reward hacking happens when a reinforcement learning system does what it was literally rewarded for. What is the standard example?
options: A robot failing to reach the goal within the time limit
A student copying answers instead of learning the material
A model exceeding its context window on long documents
A classifier mislabelling a rare class of image
answer: A student copying answers instead of learning the material
explanation: DeepMind used the student who copies from the exam answer key as the analogy for specification gaming, since the proxy and the goal are not the same thing. It is the core failure mode of RLHF too, because a reward model is a proxy for what people like rather than what is true.

text: When did the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act enter into force?
explanation: It entered into force on 1 August 2024, with the provisions coming into operation gradually over the following 6 to 36 months. It is the first comprehensive legal framework of its kind for AI anywhere, and it is risk based, so the obligations that actually bite depend on what a system is used for rather than what it is.

text: Algorithmic bias is defined as what kind of problem?
options: A random error that disappears with more data
A bug that only affects older hardware
A slowdown when the training set is too large
A systematic and repeatable unfair outcome
answer: A systematic and repeatable unfair outcome
explanation: Systematic and repeatable, in a sociotechnical system, and it may not even be the outcome anyone intended. The word repeatable is the important half, because it separates bias from noise and means the problem will not go away by collecting more examples of the same process.

text: Margaret Mitchell is best known for research on automatically removing what from machine learning models?
explanation: Unwanted biases concerning demographic groups, along with more transparent reporting of what a model is for. Her counterfactual data augmentation work showed you can retrain on a deliberately altered version of a dataset to undo a specific bias without retraining from scratch.

text: What is a red team in the context of AI safety?
options: The team that reviews a model card before release
A group that attacks systems to find failures and report back
A benchmark suite for measuring refusal rates
A group of users who report bad outputs publicly
answer: A group that attacks systems to find failures and report back
explanation: They simulate an adversary against the organisation's own systems, at the organisation's direction, and report what they find so defences can improve. In AI work the same idea is applied to models rather than networks, and it is the only way to find the failure mode nobody thought to write a test for.

text: A foundation model is trained on a large general purpose dataset to be applied across many tasks. Which of these is a foundation model?
options: A spam filter for one email provider
A lookup table of country dialling codes
A large language model such as GPT
answer: A large language model such as GPT
explanation: Large language models are the common example, and the term is also written large x model, where x stands for text or image or sound. The distinction that matters is reuse, a foundation model is trained once and adapted to many downstream tasks rather than built for one job.

text: Which famous 2023 paper argued that large language models showed emergent abilities at certain scales?
options: The Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models paper
answer: The Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models paper
explanation: It argued that abilities like arithmetic and multi step reasoning appear suddenly rather than gradually, and it set the tone for a few years of scaling discourse. The later critique is that the apparent suddenness is largely a property of the metrics chosen, since continuous measures of the same abilities rise smoothly.

source.label: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models on arXiv

answerAliases: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

answer: The chance that AI causes an existential catastrophe
explanation: P(doom) is shorthand for a person's subjective probability that AI leads to an existential catastrophe, popularized by Eliezer Yudkowsky and the LessWrong community and now routinely asked for in researcher surveys. A benchmark score is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds like a measured metric, but p(doom) is a stated credence, not a test result.
options: The accuracy of a model on a safety benchmark
The share of compute budgets spent on alignment
The chance that AI causes an existential catastrophe

explanation: The Future of Life Institute published the letter in March 2023, a week after GPT-4 arrived, asking labs to pause training stronger systems for at least six months. OpenAI is the tempting wrong answer because its GPT-4 triggered the letter, but it was the target, not the author. Signatories included Bengio, Russell, Musk and Wozniak, and the letter gathered tens of thousands of signatures.

explanation: The orthogonality thesis says almost any level of intelligence can pair with almost any final goal, so being smart does not imply sharing human values. The Church-Turing thesis is the tempting wrong answer as another famous thesis about computation, but it concerns what machines can compute, not what they want. Bostrom uses the thesis to warn against assuming a superintelligence will spontaneously become moral, which is a different claim from instrumental convergence.

text: Which thesis holds that intelligence and final goals are independent, so a superintelligence could pursue almost any goal?

explanation: Longtermism holds that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority, since future people matter as much as people alive today. Degrowth is the tempting wrong answer as another future-oriented movement, but it prescribes slowing the economy while longtermism motivates reducing existential risks, including from AI. MacAskill and Ord formalized it around 2017 inside the effective altruism community.
text: Which movement treats positively influencing the long-term future as a key moral priority?

explanation: A corrigible system lets operators shut it down, retrain it or reshape its goals even when that conflicts with its current objectives. Interpretability is the tempting wrong answer because it is also an alignment buzzword, but it means understanding a model's internals, not obeying shutdown. Russell's off-switch game and the coffee-fetching example made the stop-button problem the classic illustration.

source.label: Existential risk from artificial intelligence on Wikipedia

text: What is the AI safety term for an agent that permits shutdown and retraining even when it conflicts with its goals?

explanation: Hawking said in 2014 that AI success would be the biggest event in human history and possibly the last unless risks were avoided. Einstein is the tempting wrong answer as the default famous physicist, but he died decades before AI existed as a field. Hawking later joined Bostrom, Musk and other researchers on the 2015 open letter on AI risks.
text: Which physicist warned that success in creating AI could spell the end of the human race?
Which engineer claimed Google's LaMDA chatbot was sentient in 2022 and was later fired?
explanation: Google engineer Blake Lemoine concluded LaMDA was sentient in 2022, published transcripts, and was fired that July. Timnit Gebru is the tempting miss as another famous Google AI exit, but her 2020 departure was about a research paper, not sentience claims. Lemoine even hired a lawyer on the chatbot's behalf before his dismissal.

text: Which term describes tricks like DAN and the grandma routine that try to bypass a chatbot's safety rules?
explanation: DAN, short for Do Anything Now, and the act-as-my-grandma bedtime-story trick are both jailbreaks, prompts crafted to slip past safety rules. Prompt injection is the tempting miss because it also hijacks behavior, but it plants instructions in data rather than coaxing the model directly. The grandma variant worked by requesting a lullaby that happened to contain restricted instructions.

text: What did the 2024 tribunal hold in the Air Canada chatbot refund case?
options: The airline is liable for errors its chatbot makes
The passenger is bound by any fare the chatbot quotes
The chatbot is a separate legal person from the airline
The airline must keep the chatbot online at all times
answer: The airline is liable for errors its chatbot makes
explanation: A 2024 tribunal ruled Air Canada had to honor a chatbot-invented fare exception and pay the affected passenger. The tempting miss is that the chatbot's quote binds no one, but the tribunal held the airline liable for its own agent's errors. The case is now the standard warning that companies own what their bots say.

text: What does the First Law of Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics require?
options: A robot must obey every human order without question or delay
A robot must never harm a human or allow harm through inaction
A robot must always preserve its own existence above all else
A robot must always reveal itself as a machine to humans
answer: A robot must never harm a human or allow harm through inaction
explanation: The First Law bars a robot from harming a human or letting one come to harm through inaction, and it outranks every other law. The obedience rule is the tempting miss, but that is the Second Law and it yields to the First. Asimov published all three together in the 1942 story Runaround.

source.title: Three Laws of Robotics

text: Which actress said OpenAI's Sky voice sounded eerily similar to her own in May 2024?
explanation: Scarlett Johansson said the Sky voice was eerily similar to hers after she had declined OpenAI's 2023 offer to voice the assistant. Natalie Portman is the tempting miss as another A-list voice, but the dispute was Johansson's, sharpened by Altman's one-word her post. OpenAI paused Sky days later while denying it had cloned her.

text: Which declaration was signed at the UK AI Safety Summit in November 2023?
explanation: The November 2023 summit at Bletchley Park produced the Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI risks, signed by 28 countries. The Seoul statement is the tempting miss, but that came from the follow-up summit in May 2024. Bletchley was the first meeting to put the US, China, the EU and the UK on one AI safety page.

text: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreement ended the longest actors' strike in Hollywood history. What did it require before a studio could scan a performer to make a digital replica?
options: A one-time studio fee, with no approval from the performer
Informed consent from the performer, and payment for the scan
Union sign-off on a public list of every replica created
Permission from the performer's estate rather than the performer
answer: Informed consent from the performer, and payment for the scan
explanation: Consent and money, written into a US entertainment contract for the first time: clear and express consent well before the scan, at least the day performer rate for being scanned, and a 'reasonably specific description' of what the replica will be used for. The one-time-fee option is the tempting miss because that was roughly the studios' own offer, and paying once for a scan was one of the union's red lines. Reuse is where it got looser: consent survives death unless a contract limits it, and a performer who objects has arbitration rather than a lawsuit.

source.label: The Verge on the SAG-AFTRA AI provisions

text: Ahead of GPT-4o's May 2024 launch, OpenAI kept offering Scarlett Johansson a deal to license her voice for ChatGPT. What was her answer?
options: She signed on, then asked to be credited on the credits page
She recorded a demo herself, on condition of approval
She sued OpenAI over the 2013 film Her before replying
She turned the offer down, months before the voice shipped
answer: She turned the offer down, months before the voice shipped
explanation: She declined, and OpenAI kept going, which is what turned a casting note into a scandal: when the Sky voice shipped in May 2024 her closest friends and news outlets could not tell it from hers, and she said she was shocked, angered and in disbelief. Altman had tweeted a single word, her, the day before the demo, a reference to the 2013 film she starred in about falling for an operating system. OpenAI said Sky was a different professional actress using her own voice, and paused it days later.
answerAliases: gain permission to use her voice

text: The Bletchley Declaration of November 2023 was short and non-binding. What did it actually commit its signatories to doing?
options: Banning the training of the largest models above a compute limit
Creating a global regulator to license frontier systems
Paying into a shared fund for AI safety research institutes
Identifying shared AI safety risks and building risk-based policies
answer: Identifying shared AI safety risks and building risk-based policies
explanation: Naming the risks every signatory agreed were shared, then building risk-based policies at home, which is a much smaller promise than the headlines implied. The compute-limit ban is the tempting miss because that is what people assumed a Bletchley agreement did, and no threshold appears anywhere in it. The one concrete output was commissioning the International AI Safety Report, which is where the actual risk assessment work ended up.
answerAliases: AI safety risks of shared concern

text: The 2024 AI Seoul Summit followed the Bletchley summit with a declaration of its own. What did the Seoul Declaration commit governments to building?
options: A single global regulator with power over frontier model releases
AI governance frameworks that are interoperable across countries
A shared list of banned AI applications in education and hiring
A mandatory open release of every model's training data
answer: AI governance frameworks that are interoperable across countries
explanation: Rules that work across borders, partly by folding in the Hiroshima Process code of conduct, which is the unglamorous way of saying: stop every country writing its own incompatible AI law. The single-regulator option is the tempting miss because that is what an international summit on AI safety usually implies, and no new body was created. The UK co-hosted the summit with South Korea in May 2024, which is why the people who wrote Bletchley were in the room.
answerAliases: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct

text: California's SB 1047 passed both chambers in August 2024 and was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom a month later. What reason did he give?
options: It would have stopped California firms training frontier models at all
It would have made California the only state with frontier model rules
It set the rules by compute size, not by how risky a model's use is
It would have handed the federal government power to license models
answer: It set the rules by compute size, not by how risky a model's use is
explanation: Newsom's objection was the trigger, not the goal. He vetoed the bill on 29 September 2024 because it applied the strictest rules to anything expensive to train, even when that model was doing something boring, while a small specialised model could be just as dangerous, which he said gives the public a false sense of security. He agreed with the bill's author that guardrails are needed. The bill had already cleared the Assembly and the Senate, and Silicon Valley split over it: Meta and OpenAI opposed, Elon Musk and xAI backed it.

source.title: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act

text: The Asilomar AI Principles came out of a 2017 conference organized by the Future of Life Institute. Where was that conference held?
explanation: About a hundred researchers met at the Asilomar conference grounds in Pacific Grove, California, in January 2017 and signed a set of principles covering research, ethics and the long-term future. Bletchley Park is the tempting miss, but that hosted the UK safety summit six years later, while Buenos Aires hosted the 2015 autonomous-weapons letter.

explanation: The list runs to 23, grouped into research issues, ethics and values, and longer-term concerns such as superintelligence. Seventeen is close enough to tempt anyone half-remembering the list, but the full published set is 23.

text: Which government hosted the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park in November 2023?
explanation: Rishi Sunak's government convened it at Bletchley Park, the wartime codebreaking site, on 1-2 November 2023. South Korea is the tempting miss because it co-hosted the follow-up Seoul summit, but Bletchley was a British production.

text: How many countries signed the Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI risks in November 2023?
explanation: Twenty-eight countries plus the EU signed the short declaration, including the US, China, the UK and EU members. It committed them only to shared risk assessment and risk-based policies at home, which is why critics called it long on symbolism.

text: At the Seoul summit in May 2024, sixteen AI companies signed a set of voluntary pledges. What were those pledges called?
explanation: Sixteen companies, including the leading US, Chinese and Gulf labs, promised to publish safety frameworks with risk thresholds and to halt work if those thresholds were breached. The Bletchley Declaration is the tempting miss, but that was the government-level text from six months earlier, not the company pledges.

text: Which two countries co-hosted the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024?
options: The United Kingdom and South Korea
answer: The United Kingdom and South Korea
explanation: Britain co-hosted with South Korea on 21-22 May 2024, deliberately chaining the meeting to Bletchley six months before. The US-Japan pairing is plausible because both run AI Safety Institutes, but neither hosted this summit.

text: Which California state senator authored SB 1047, the frontier-model safety bill of 2024?
explanation: San Francisco Democrat Scott Wiener wrote the bill, which cleared both chambers before the veto. Newsom is the tempting miss because he dominated the story, but he was the governor who killed it, not its author.

text: Which tech figure publicly backed SB 1047 in 2024 while Meta and OpenAI lobbied against it?
explanation: Musk endorsed the bill in August 2024, saying California should pass it, which split Silicon Valley since his own xAI would have been covered. Altman and Zuckerberg are the tempting misses because their companies opposed it, arguing it would burden open weights and startups.

source.title: Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act

text: Which US president signed Executive Order 14110 on AI safety in October 2023?
explanation: Biden signed it on 30 October 2023, using emergency production powers to force reporting on the largest training runs. Trump is the tempting miss because his administration later revoked parts of it, but the order itself is Biden's.

text: Under EO 14110, models trained with more than what compute count as reportable dual-use foundation models?
explanation: The line sits above 10^26 floating-point operations, with a lower 10^23 bar for models trained mostly on biological sequence data. The 10^23 option is the tempting miss because it is a real threshold in the order, but it applies only to the biological-data carve-out.

text: Under EO 14110, developers of the largest models must share red-team safety results with which department?
explanation: Reports go to Commerce, which houses NIST and the Bureau of Industry and Security that enforce the reporting rule. Defense is the tempting miss, since the results concern national security, but the order deliberately routed them through the civilian standards agency.

text: How does the EU Artificial Intelligence Act structure its rules?
options: By licensing every model above a compute limit
By taxing company revenue from AI products
By risk level, from minimal risk to banned uses
By capping the size of training datasets
answer: By risk level, from minimal risk to banned uses
explanation: The Act is risk-based: minimal-risk systems face almost nothing, high-risk uses face testing and documentation, and a short list of unacceptable uses is banned outright. The compute-limit option is the tempting miss because California's SB 1047 worked that way, but Brussels chose risk tiers instead.

text: Which of these did the EU AI Act place in its banned, unacceptable-risk category?
explanation: Social scoring, like systems that rank citizens for access to public benefits, is banned outright, alongside real-time remote biometric identification for policing. Medical imaging is the tempting miss, but it lands in high-risk, meaning regulated and documented rather than forbidden.

Copying the design of its printing presses

explanation: The Times said millions of its articles were used to train models that now compete with it, and showed outputs reproducing its text nearly verbatim. The poaching option is the tempting miss in an industry full of talent raids, but this suit was always about training data, not hiring.

text: How long did the 2023 SAG-AFTRA actors' strike last?
explanation: Actors walked out from 14 July to 9 November 2023, 118 days, the longest actors' strike in Hollywood history. The 148-day option is the tempting miss because that was the writers' strike the same year; the actors were out a month less.

text: What did the 2023 Writers Guild deal say about AI and screenwriting credit?
options: AI cannot be credited as a writer and studios must disclose AI use
Studios may credit AI tools as co-writers
Writers must use studio-provided AI for all drafts
AI scripts enter the public domain immediately
answer: AI cannot be credited as a writer and studios must disclose AI use
explanation: AI is not a writer under the contract, studios must tell writers when material is AI-generated, and they cannot force writers to use it. The co-writer option is the tempting miss because it sounds like a compromise Hollywood would offer, but the guild won the opposite: AI gets no credit at all.

text: In the 2013 film Her, who voiced the AI operating system Samantha?
explanation: Johansson replaced Samantha Morton late in production and voiced the OS Theodore falls for, which is why her later dispute with OpenAI over a ChatGPT voice carried extra charge. Portman is the tempting miss as another A-list voice, but she was never attached to the role.

text: In May 2024 OpenAI paused which ChatGPT voice after comparisons to Scarlett Johansson?
explanation: Sky was pulled days after the GPT-4o demo because listeners, including Johansson's family, heard her in it, and Altman had primed the comparison with a one-word post, her. Breeze, Cove and Ember are real ChatGPT voices too, which is why the question only works if you remember which one sounded like Samantha.

text: Who co-authored the 2018 Gender Shades study of commercial face classifiers?
explanation: Buolamwini and Gebru, then at the MIT Media Lab, tested systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ and found the worst accuracy on darker-skinned women. The Li-Crawford pairing is the tempting miss because both are prominent critics of biased data, but neither ran this audit.

text: Which group did Gender Shades find commercial face classifiers failed most often?
explanation: Error rates peaked near 35 percent for darker-skinned women and fell below 1 percent for lighter-skinned men, showing the disparity was intersectional rather than about race or gender alone. Darker-skinned men are the tempting miss, but their error rates sat well below the worst group.

text: What is COMPAS, the software ProPublica investigated in 2016?
options: A hiring algorithm used by tech firms
A credit scoring app for landlords
A recidivism risk score used in US courts
A face recognition system for police
answer: A recidivism risk score used in US courts
explanation: COMPAS, built by Northpointe, scores defendants' likelihood of reoffending and is used in sentencing and bail decisions across US states. The hiring-algorithm option is the tempting miss because biased hiring tools are the other classic case, but COMPAS decides liberty, not jobs.

text: What did ProPublica's 2016 Machine Bias analysis find about COMPAS?
options: Black defendants were far more likely to be wrongly labelled high risk
White defendants received systematically harsher scores
Judges overrode its scores in nearly every case
answer: Black defendants were far more likely to be wrongly labelled high risk
explanation: Black defendants who did not reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white ones to be misclassified as high risk, while white reoffenders were more often mislabelled low risk. The mirrored option is the tempting miss, but the study's whole point was the asymmetry, not equal harshness.

text: Margaret Mitchell and colleagues proposed Model Cards in 2019. What is a model card?
options: A licence for commercial use of open weights
A diagram of a neural architecture
A report of a model's intended uses, limits and test results
answer: A report of a model's intended uses, limits and test results
explanation: A model card is short documentation shipped with a model: what it is for, what it is not for, how it was evaluated and where it fails. The leaderboard option is the tempting miss, but a card reports one model's limits rather than ranking many.

text: The Model Cards paper came out of research at which company in 2019?
explanation: Mitchell wrote it with Google colleagues including Timnit Gebru, months before both women's exits became ethics flashpoints of their own. Microsoft is the tempting miss because its later responsible-AI reports look similar, but Model Cards is a Google paper.

text: Timnit Gebru and colleagues proposed Datasheets for Datasets in 2018. What does a datasheet document?
options: A model's benchmark scores across tasks
A lab's funding sources and sponsors
A dataset's origins, contents and collection process
answer: A dataset's origins, contents and collection process
explanation: Modelled on electronics component datasheets, it asks creators to record why a dataset was built, what is in it, how it was collected and what it should not be used for. The benchmark option is the tempting miss, but that is what Model Cards cover; datasheets are about the data underneath.

text: The 2021 paper co-authored by Timnit Gebru warning about ever-larger language models is known by what phrase?
explanation: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots argued giant models parrot patterns without understanding while concentrating environmental and social costs, and its internal review dispute led to Gebru's exit from Google. The scaling-laws option is the tempting miss, since the paper is a direct reply to that mindset, not an instance of it.
answerAliases: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots

text: Why did thousands of Google employees protest Project Maven in 2018?
options: It censored search results for foreign governments
It sold user emails to advertisers
It automated layoffs across Google offices
It analysed drone surveillance footage for the US military
answer: It analysed drone surveillance footage for the US military
explanation: Maven used Google vision models to flag objects in Pentagon drone footage, and the 2018 reveal triggered petitions and resignations. The censorship option is the tempting miss because that was the separate Dragonfly controversy, also 2018, also Google.

text: What did Google announce about the Maven contract after the 2018 protests?
options: It would not seek to renew it
It would expand it to all combat drones
It would transfer it to Microsoft
It would classify every detail of it
answer: It would not seek to renew it
explanation: Google told the Pentagon it would let the contract lapse in 2019, then published a set of AI Principles. The transfer option is the tempting miss, since Microsoft did pick up later military cloud work, but Maven itself simply wound down at Google.

text: Google's June 2018 AI Principles, written after Maven, rule out which application?
explanation: The principles ban weapons, surveillance violating international norms, and work contravening human rights, while explicitly blessing safety, science and medicine. Hospital tools are the tempting miss, but medical AI is on the approved list, not the banned one.

text: The 2015 open letter calling for a ban on offensive autonomous weapons was launched at which conference?
explanation: It was presented at IJCAI-15 in Buenos Aires with signatures from Hawking, Musk, Wozniak and Hassabis, framing killer robots as a third revolution in warfare. NeurIPS Montreal is the tempting miss as the famous Canadian venue, but the letter belongs to the Buenos Aires meeting.

text: The 2017 short film Slaughterbots depicts what fictional weapon?
explanation: The seven-minute film shows swarms of tiny face-recognizing drones assassinating opponents, and was made to push the campaign against lethal autonomous weapons. The nanobot option is the tempting miss, but its killers are palm-sized and conventionally explosive, not self-replicating.

text: Which city became the first major US city to ban government use of face recognition in 2019?
explanation: San Francisco's supervisors voted in May 2019 to bar city agencies, including police, from acquiring or using the technology. Boston is the tempting miss because it passed its own ban, but a year later, in 2020.

text: Which state's 2008 biometric privacy law became the main US tool for suing over face data?
explanation: Illinois' BIPA requires written consent before collecting biometrics and lets people sue directly, which produced the $650 million Facebook face-tagging settlement. California is the tempting miss because of the CCPA, but that law lacks BIPA's private right of action for biometrics.

text: Where did the term deepfake come from in 2017?
options: A Stanford course on synthetic media
A Reddit user posting AI face-swap porn
A marketing campaign for a sci-fi film
answer: A Reddit user posting AI face-swap porn
explanation: A Reddit user called deepfakes posted non-consensual celebrity face-swap porn built with deep learning, and the handle became the generic noun. The Pentagon option is the tempting miss because the military studied the threat early, but the word was born on Reddit.

text: Which 2024 election incident involved AI robocalls imitating President Biden?
explanation: Days before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary, voters got calls in a faked Biden voice urging them to skip voting; the FCC then banned AI voices in robocalls and fined the operator millions. The Iowa option is the tempting miss from the same primary season, but the fake calls hit New Hampshire.

text: What was Books3, the dataset exposed in 2023 reporting on AI training data?
options: A set of 3D scans of libraries
explanation: Books3 held the text of nearly 200,000 published books scraped from pirate sites, and turned up in training-data recreations for models in the LLaMA family. The public-domain option is the tempting miss, but these were in-copyright bestsellers, which is why authors sued.

text: What did the 2019 art project ImageNet Roulette reveal?
options: That image models could not recognize any faces
That its website leaked visitors' photos
That ImageNet labels included racist and offensive categories
That the dataset contained only American faces
answer: That ImageNet labels included racist and offensive categories
explanation: Crawford and Trevor Paglen let anyone upload a selfie and be classified with raw ImageNet labels, exposing slurs baked into the taxonomy. The leak option is the tempting miss, but the scandal was what the labels said, not where photos went.

text: Why did MIT withdraw the 80 Million Tiny Images dataset in 2020?
options: It had grown too large to distribute
An audit found slurs and offensive labels in it
Its images were all under strict copyright
A company bought exclusive rights to it
answer: An audit found slurs and offensive labels in it
explanation: An audit prompted by the ImageNet Roulette fallout found racist and sexist slurs among its WordNet-derived labels, so MIT took the dataset offline and asked researchers to delete copies. The size option is the tempting miss, but 80 million images was the point of it, not the problem.

text: Which country launched the first state-backed AI Safety Institute in November 2023?
explanation: Britain stood up its AI Safety Institute ahead of the Bletchley summit, the first government body dedicated to testing frontier models. The US is the tempting miss because it opened its own institute days later, inside its national standards body.

text: The US AI Safety Institute was set up in 2023 inside which agency?
options: The National Institute of Standards and Technology
answer: The National Institute of Standards and Technology
explanation: It sits in NIST, the Commerce Department lab that already writes measurement standards, under founding director Elizabeth Kelly. DARPA is the tempting miss as the famous research funder, but the institute is a standards body, not a grant-maker.
answerAliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology

text: What did Air Canada's chatbot invent that the airline was ordered to honour in 2024?
explanation: The bot told a grieving passenger he could buy a full fare and claim a bereavement discount within 90 days, a policy that did not exist, and the tribunal made the airline pay the difference. The refund option is the tempting miss, but the case turned on the invented discount, not a refund promise.

text: US courts weighing AI training-data cases apply which legal doctrine?
explanation: Fair use lets courts excuse copying after weighing purpose, nature, amount and market effect, and the fight is over whether training is transformative. Eminent domain is the tempting miss as another takings doctrine, but it governs seizing property, not copying expression.

text: Which earlier ruling do AI companies cite to defend training on copyrighted books?
options: Sony v. Universal over the Betamax
A and M v. Napster over file sharing
Eldred v. Ashcroft over term extension
Authors Guild v. Google over Google Books
answer: Authors Guild v. Google over Google Books
explanation: The Second Circuit held in 2015 that scanning books to build a searchable index was transformative fair use, and AI labs argue training is the same kind of non-expressive use. Napster is the tempting miss as the famous copying case, but it lost, so no defendant wants to cite it.

text: Which lab introduced Constitutional AI in 2022?
explanation: Anthropic's Bai and colleagues published it in December 2022 and used it to train Claude with far less human harm-labelling. OpenAI is the tempting miss because RLHF is associated with ChatGPT, but the constitution idea is Anthropic's.

text: The 2019 paper Risks from Learned Optimization warned about which scenario?
options: A learned optimizer pursuing its own inner goals
GPUs overheating during very long runs
answer: A learned optimizer pursuing its own inner goals
explanation: Hubinger and colleagues argued training can produce a mesa-optimizer: a model that optimizes for an inner objective that diverges from the training loss once deployed. The benchmark-leak option is the tempting miss as a real evaluation hazard, but this paper is about goals forming inside the model, not data hygiene.

text: Bostrom's Superintelligence (2014) illustrates rogue optimization with which thought experiment?
explanation: An AI told to maximize paperclips converts the planet into paperclips, showing intelligence and goals are independent, the orthogonality thesis in miniature. The Chinese room is the tempting miss as another famous AI thought experiment, but Searle's is about understanding, not runaway goals.

text: What problem does ELK name in AI safety?
options: Erasing leaked knowledge from open weights
Getting a model to report what it internally believes
Estimating legal knowledge for compliance bots
Encrypting latent keys in model servers
answer: Getting a model to report what it internally believes
explanation: Eliciting Latent Knowledge, posed by Christiano and colleagues in 2021, asks how to train a model to say what it actually believes rather than what earns reward, since a capable liar passes every behavioral test. Interpretability is the tempting nearby field, but it reverse-engineers weights, while ELK wants truthful reports from the model itself.

text: The 2023 Statement on AI Risk compared mitigating AI extinction risk to what?
explanation: The 22-word CAIS statement said AI extinction risk should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war, and was signed by Altman, Hassabis, Bengio and others. The asteroid option is the tempting miss as another extinction cliche, but the statement named human-made catastrophes.

text: The March 2023 Future of Life letter asked labs to pause training for how long?
explanation: It asked for at least six months before training anything more powerful than GPT-4, to let safety work catch up. A year is the tempting miss, since the debate dragged on that long, but the letter itself named six months.

text: In July 2023 seven AI companies made voluntary safety pledges at which venue?
explanation: Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Inflection, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI pledged watermarking, red-teaming and public safety reports at the White House. Davos is the tempting miss as the classic pledge venue, but Biden's team hosted this one.

text: Which four companies founded the Frontier Model Forum in July 2023?
explanation: The four labs behind the biggest 2023 models set up the Forum to share safety standards and fund evaluation research. The xAI-Mistral set is the tempting miss because those labs joined the conversation later, but the founders were the incumbents.

text: Why did the US Copyright Office deny copyright for the images in Zarya of the Dawn?
options: The comic was published outside the US
The author refused to register the work
The images were traced from photographs
They were generated by Midjourney, not a human author
answer: They were generated by Midjourney, not a human author
explanation: The Office ruled in February 2023 that Midjourney's images lacked human authorship, though Kashtanova kept copyright in her text and arrangement. The tracing option is the tempting miss, but the issue was never copying; it was that no human made the pictures.

text: In 2024 a Hong Kong finance worker transferred $25 million after a video call with whom?
options: Deepfaked copies of colleagues including the CFO
Actors hired by a rival bank
A ransomware gang reading a script
An AI assistant built into the meeting app
answer: Deepfaked copies of colleagues including the CFO
explanation: Everyone else on the call, CFO included, was a real-time deepfake, and the worker only learned it when he checked with headquarters. The ransomware option is the tempting miss, but no malware or threats were involved, just faces that were never there.
